meta.title: Who originally recorded "The Girl from Ipanema"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Stan Getz and Astrud Gilberto. Pery Ribeiro made the first commercial recording in Brazil in 1962; the Verve version came out in March 1964.
meta.ogTitle: Who originally recorded 'The Girl from Ipanema'?
meta.ogDescription: Pery Ribeiro recorded it for Odeon in 1962. Getz and Gilberto taped their version in March 1963 and Verve released it in March 1964.

answer.label: Not a Stan Getz and Astrud Gilberto original — Pery Ribeiro cut it in Brazil first, in 1962
answer.originalArtistDates: 1937-2012 · Brazilian bossa nova and MPB singer, son of Dalva de Oliveira and Herivelto Martins
answer.sourceLine: Almost everyone meets this song through the Stan Getz and Astrud Gilberto recording, and treats that record as the song’s birth. It isn’t. “Garota de Ipanema” was written in 1962 by Antônio Carlos Jobim (music) and Vinícius de Moraes (Portuguese lyrics), and the first commercial recording was made that year by the Brazilian singer Pery Ribeiro, issued by Odeon and collected on his LP Pery é Todo Bossa. Norman Gimbel’s English lyric came afterwards, for the international version. Getz and João Gilberto did not tape their Getz/Gilberto session until 18–19 March 1963, and Verve did not release the album until March 1964.

original.label: Odeon (Brazil)
original.released: Recorded in 1962 for Odeon and issued in Brazil in January 1963; collected on Ribeiro’s LP Pery é Todo Bossa (1963). Universal’s own distribution metadata for the album track gives a release date of 5 January 1963 and a ℗ 1963 EMI Records Brasil line.
original.charted: No US or UK chart placing. It was a domestic Brazilian release sung in Portuguese and never issued into the American market.
original.writer: Antônio Carlos Jobim (music); Vinícius de Moraes (Portuguese lyrics); Norman Gimbel (English lyrics)
original.cover: Stan Getz and Astrud Gilberto, from the album Getz/Gilberto — recorded 18-19 March 1963 in New York, released by Verve in March 1964. The single edit peaked at number 5 on the Billboard Hot 100 and won the Grammy for Record of the Year in 1965.

trail: English Wikipedia ↗ states that the first commercial recording was made in 1962 by Pery Ribeiro, and credits the music to Jobim, the Portuguese lyric to Vinícius de Moraes and the English lyric to Norman Gimbel.

Portuguese Wikipedia ↗ gives the Brazilian side: Ribeiro’s Odeon recording, a near-simultaneous Tamba Trio release on Philips in January 1963, and the song’s live run at the Au Bon Gourmet club in Rio.
The Getz/Gilberto entry ↗ dates the famous session to 18-19 March 1963 at A&R Recording Studios and the Verve release to March 1964 — both after Ribeiro’s record was already in Brazilian shops.
A MusicBrainz work entry ↗ ties every version to the same Jobim/de Moraes composition, and its Ribeiro recording carries a 1963 first release on Pery é todo bossa.

authors.name: Pery Ribeiro
authors.heading: Pery Ribeiro
authors.bio: Born Peri Oliveira Martins in Rio de Janeiro in 1937, Ribeiro came from Brazilian musical royalty — his mother was the singer Dalva de Oliveira and his father the songwriter Herivelto Martins. He was one of the first voices of bossa nova on record, and in 1962 he made the first commercial recording of “Garota de Ipanema” for Odeon; it landed on his 1963 LP Pery é Todo Bossa. He kept singing until his death in Rio in 2012, and Rolling Stone Brasil placed him 64th among the country’s hundred greatest singers ↗.

authors.name: Stan Getz and Astrud Gilberto
authors.heading: Stan Getz & Astrud Gilberto
authors.bio: The version the world knows was taped in New York on 18 and 19 March 1963 for the album Getz/Gilberto, with Stan Getz on tenor saxophone, João Gilberto on guitar and vocal, Jobim himself at the piano, and João’s wife Astrud Gilberto singing the English lyric — her recording debut. Verve released it in March 1964; the single reached number 5 on the US Billboard Hot 100 and took the 1965 Grammy for Record of the Year, while the album became the first non-American record to win Album of the Year. It is a genuinely great record, and it deserves nearly all of its reputation. The only thing it is not is the first.

authors.name: Jobim, Moraes and Gimbel
authors.heading: Jobim, de Moraes & Gimbel
authors.bio: Antônio Carlos Jobim wrote the music at his home near Rua Barão da Torre in Ipanema; the poet and diplomat Vinícius de Moraes wrote the Portuguese lyric. The melody began life for a musical comedy under a different working title before it became the song we know. Norman Gimbel, the American lyricist, supplied the separate English words that Astrud Gilberto sang — which is why the Portuguese and English versions are not translations of one another so much as two lyrics fitted to one tune.

misattribution.heading: Right song, wrong first record
misattribution.intro: The Getz/Gilberto single is one of the most-played recordings ever made, which is exactly why it gets mistaken for the beginning of the story rather than a chapter of it.

items.why: Recorded in New York on 18-19 March 1963 and released by Verve in March 1964. It reached number 5 on the Billboard Hot 100 and won the 1965 Grammy for Record of the Year — but it was not the first recording.
The Brazilian singer made the first commercial recording of “Garota de Ipanema” in 1962 for Odeon; it was issued in Brazil in January 1963 and appeared on his LP Pery é Todo Bossa.

items.who: Antônio Carlos Jobim, Vinícius de Moraes and Norman Gimbel
items.why: Jobim wrote the music and de Moraes the Portuguese lyric, both in 1962. Norman Gimbel wrote the separate English lyric used on the Getz/Gilberto recording.
Portuguese-language sources record a Tamba Trio version issued on Philips at the same moment as Ribeiro’s in January 1963, the two labels releasing together to avoid a dispute.

misattribution.truthLine: Pery Ribeiro recorded it first, in Brazil, in 1962. Getz and Gilberto made it famous two years later.

context.heading: Why the cover swallowed the original
lead: The interesting question is not why Getz and Gilberto had the hit — it is why the Brazilian original vanished so completely from the story. Part of the answer is that Pery Ribeiro’s record was a domestic Brazilian release on Odeon, sung in Portuguese, made for a Rio audience that already knew the song from the bossa nova circuit. It was never aimed at America and never travelled there.

The other part is that Getz/Gilberto arrived with everything the original lacked: an American label, a saxophone star, an English lyric written specifically for export, and a singer — Astrud Gilberto, at the microphone for the first time in her life — whose unpolished delivery turned out to be exactly the sound the record needed. A Grammy for Record of the Year does the rest. Once a song wins the biggest award in American music, the recording that won it becomes, in the popular mind, the recording that started it.
detailsBody: 1962 — Jobim writes the music and Vinícius de Moraes the Portuguese lyric; the song is performed in Rio during the bossa nova run at the Au Bon Gourmet nightclub.
1962 — Pery Ribeiro records the first commercial version, for Odeon.

January 1963 — the Ribeiro recording is issued in Brazil; his LP Pery é Todo Bossa follows the same year. Portuguese-language sources note a near-simultaneous Brazilian release by Tamba Trio on Philips, timed to avoid a dispute between the labels.
18-19 March 1963 — Stan Getz, João Gilberto, Astrud Gilberto and Jobim record Getz/Gilberto at A&R Recording Studios in New York, produced by Creed Taylor, using Norman Gimbel’s English lyric.
March 1964 — Verve releases Getz/Gilberto. The single edit reaches number 5 on the Billboard Hot 100.
1965 — “The Girl from Ipanema” wins the Grammy for Record of the Year, and the album wins Album of the Year.
context.pull: Ribeiro sang it first; Verve simply sang it louder, in English, to a bigger room.
